title: Container secrets
description: Handle API keys, database passwords, and TLS certificates safely inside containers using Docker secrets, environment variables, and mounted secrets.

data.text: Every production container needs secrets: database passwords, API keys, TLS certificates, and OAuth client secrets. The way you pass these secrets into a container determines whether an attacker who gains access to the container can also access your production database, third-party APIs, or certificate authorities.
Why environment variables are not secrets

Environment variables are the most common way to pass configuration to containers, but they are not a security control. Environment variables are visible in `docker inspect`, in process listings inside the container, and in crash dumps. They are also often logged accidentally by application frameworks.

data.title: Environment variables leak easily
data.text: Anyone with access to the Docker host can run `docker inspect <container>` and read every environment variable, including secrets. Logging frameworks, crash reporters, and error pages may also print environment variables into logs or error output.

Docker secrets are designed specifically for sensitive data. A secret is stored encrypted in the Raft log of a Docker Swarm manager and is decrypted only inside the containers that receive it. On Linux, secrets are exposed as in-memory files under `/run/secrets/<name>` rather than as environment variables, which makes accidental logging less likely.

data.title: Using Docker secrets with Compose
data.content: This Compose file defines a secret from a local file and mounts it into the container.
data.code:
services:
  database:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD_FILE: /run/secrets/db_password
    secrets:
      - db_password
    networks:
      - data
    read_only: true
    tmpfs:
      - /tmp
      - /run/postgresql

secrets:
  db_password:
    file: ./secrets/db_password.txt

networks:
  data:
    internal: true

data.title: Docker secrets rules
items: Secrets require Swarm mode. Enable it with `docker swarm init` on at least one manager node
Secrets are scoped to services. A service can only access secrets explicitly listed in its `secrets` section
Secret files appear under /run/secrets/<name> in the container, not as environment variables
Secret files are stored in a tmpfs mount and never written to the container's writable layer

data.text: In Kubernetes, secrets are API objects. By default they are stored as base64-encoded strings in etcd, which means you must encrypt etcd at rest. Kubernetes can inject secrets as environment variables or as mounted files. Mounted files are generally safer because they do not appear in process environment tables.

data.title: Kubernetes secret as a mounted file
data.content: This Pod spec mounts a Kubernetes secret as a file at /run/secrets/db-password.
data.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: database-client
spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: myapp:latest
      volumeMounts:
        - name: db-password
          mountPath: /run/secrets
          readOnly: true
      env:
        - name: DB_PASSWORD_FILE
          value: /run/secrets/db-password
  volumes:
    - name: db-password
      secret:
        secretName: db-password

data.text: For large-scale deployments, use a dedicated secret manager such as HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, or Google Secret Manager. These tools provide audit logging, automatic rotation, fine-grained access control, and encryption at rest without requiring you to store secrets in container definitions.

cards.title: Docker secrets
cards.description: Built-in encrypted storage for Swarm clusters.
pros: Encrypted in transit and at rest

cards.title: Kubernetes secrets
cards.description: Native Kubernetes secret objects with base64 encoding.
pros: Works with operators and CSI drivers
cons: Mount as env vars is risky

cards.title: External secret manager
cards.description: Dedicated services such as Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, or Azure Key Vault.

data.text: As your application grows, the number of secrets grows. Secret sprawl makes rotation difficult, auditing impossible, and breaches catastrophic. Follow these rules to keep secrets under control.

data.title: Secret hygiene rules
items: Store secrets in a single secret manager, not scattered across environment variables, config files, and CI/CD variables
Rotate secrets on a regular schedule and after any suspected exposure
Scope secrets to the minimum set of services that need them
Never commit secrets to version control, including private repositories
Scan repositories for accidentally committed secrets with tools such as gitleaks or trufflehog

data.title: Key takeaways
points: Environment variables are not secrets; they are visible to anyone with Docker host access
Docker secrets encrypt secrets at rest and inject them as files in Swarm
Kubernetes secrets require etcd encryption and should be mounted as files
External secret managers provide rotation, auditing, and fine-grained access control
Never commit secrets to version control or store them in Docker images
data.takeaway: Secrets belong in a dedicated secret manager, not in environment variables, config files, or Docker images.
